# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is lazy. Left alone, it sits still, and if you want it to move—to flow through pipes, up a building, out of a faucet on the fortieth floor—you have to give it a reason. The entire engineering discipline of water distribution is, at its heart, the management of one simple physical fact: water only flows where pressure pushes it. Understanding how a modern city moves water from a reservoir to the top of a skyscraper means understanding where that pressure comes from, how it's measured, and how engineers keep it steady even as millions of people open and close their taps.

## The Free Ride: Elevation Head

The cheapest pressure in any water system is the pressure you get for free from gravity. Engineers call this "elevation head," and it works like this: a column of water generates about 0.433 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure for every foot of height. If your water source sits 100 feet above your faucet, the water arrives at your tap with roughly 43 psi of pressure behind it, before friction losses in the pipes take their toll.

This is why cities are so deliberate about where they place their reservoirs
